`if:` and `success_when:` conditions: operators, truthiness, fallbacks for a missing value, and what a skipped branch does.

**`if:` conditions.** A condition is one comparison (`==` or `=`, `!=`, `>=`, `<=`, `>`, `<`), a bare value (truthy test), or an expression joining them with `&&`, `||`, `!` and parentheses: `if: ${{ steps.call.outputs.status }} >= 200 && ${{ steps.call.outputs.status }} < 300`, `if: ${{ !steps.x.outputs.rows }}`, `if: ${{ a == 1 && b == 0 }}`. Semantics are JavaScript's: comparisons bind tighter than `&&`, which binds tighter than `||`; `&&` and `||` short-circuit and return an operand, so `a || 'x'` is the first truthy operand (a fallback) and `||` is also the connective; `!` negates. One operator per comparison (`a < b < c` doesn't parse). Truthy means true, non-empty, non-zero: an empty string, `0`, `false`, `no`, `null`, a missing ref and an empty result set are falsy. The condition you wrote is parsed before any value is substituted, and a substituted value is only ever an operand, so a request value such as `!=x` or `' || '1` is compared as text and can never change the condition. `>=`/`<=`/`>`/`<` compare numerically when both sides are numbers (`9 > 10` is false) and as text otherwise; `==`/`!=` compare text (`50 == 50.0` is false). In an expression, quote text literals: a bare word is a ref. In a single comparison a `steps.`/`params.`/`user.`/`env.` ref is a ref on either side, `${{ params.token == steps.t.outputs.token }}` and `${{ steps.doc.outputs.owner_id != user.id }}` included; a literal on the left (`${{ 5 < params.n }}`) compares the ref with it. A ref with no value is empty against a literal, but never equals a request field when it is a step output, and equals nothing on the right of a single comparison: when no branch runs, the `if:` step fails with a 500 (missing_values). Test for the row first: `if: ${{ steps.t.outputs.rows }} && ${{ params.token == steps.t.outputs.token }}`. A condition that doesn't parse evaluates false and is logged once; so a deny guard written that way (`if: ${{ !contains(params.role, 'admin') }}` → respond 403) never fires. The write gate and `benmore check` refuse an `if:`, `success_when:` or templated serve_file `disposition:` that can never be true (it doesn't parse, or a single comparison's left side is neither a field nor a ref), naming the step; a file already deployed still loads. In a condition that is one comparison or operator-less, the `||` inside a ref is a fallback: `${{ a || b || '' }} == ''`, and a bare `a || 'x' == 'x'` compares the fallback (inside an expression write `${{ a || 'x' }} == 'x'`). `success_when:` takes the same conditions. Hook and workflow `when:` are SQL instead: api({at:'hooks'}) → when_conditions.

**Operator-less `if:` on an OPTIONAL param is JS-truthy.** `if: ${{ params.invite_token }}` is FALSE when the param is absent OR empty-string, and `| default:` / `||` apply inside the condition too: `if: ${{ params.invite_token | default:'' }}` and `if: ${{ params.invite_token || '' }}` are both FALSE when the token is missing/empty, TRUE when it has a value (or a non-empty fallback). So `if: ${{ params.x }}` is the clean 'was this optional field supplied?' guard - no `!= ''` comparison is needed. Bare literals (`true`/`1`/`'x'`) are judged literally.

**A skipped `if:` branch does NOT evaluate its body** - and a bare `if: ${{ steps.x.outputs.rows }}` is FALSE on an empty result (empty arrays/objects/`"[]"` are falsy). So guard a 'has rows' branch with `if: ${{ steps.x.outputs.rows }}` directly and reference `rows[0]` safely inside it - no COUNT(*)/COALESCE workaround needed.

**Missing/absent refs have a fallback - no need to always-send a field.** `${{ params.x | default:'v' }}` AND `${{ params.x || 'v' }}` both yield the fallback when `x` is absent from the request OR empty. The `||` right side is a quoted literal or another ref (`a || b || 'c'`).
